fixes.explanation: Yes, idols, baker. "With their silver and gold they make themselves idols, to their own destruction." They spent the good stuff on things that couldn't help them. Silver and gold went in, and idols came out. That's like pouring your whole paycheck into a toaster that doesn't toast.
True. God says, "For this thing is from Israel—a craftsman made it, and it is not God." So the calf came from a craftsman, not from God. Something somebody made can't be the One who made them.

I can see why you'd think an idol would last. But God says the opposite: "It will be broken to pieces, that calf of Samaria." Nothing in the verse says it stands for years. Broken to pieces is the whole forecast.

No storing happens in this verse. God says, "Even if it should produce, the foreigners would swallow it up." If the fields do give anything, the verse says foreigners would swallow it up. Setting it aside for later isn't mentioned.

That would be a happy ending, but it isn't in this verse. The text says, "Even if it should produce, the foreigners would swallow it up." If the fields do produce, it's foreigners who swallow it up. Sharing never comes up.
Assyria, yes. "For they have gone up to Assyria like a wild donkey on its own." The verse compares Israel to a wild donkey on its own. And the place they go up to is Assyria.

Strange is the word. "Though I wrote for them the great things of My law, they regarded them as something strange." God wrote them out, and Israel regarded them as something strange. I think that stings.
Egypt. God says, "They will return to Egypt." That comes right after He says He will "…remember their iniquity and punish their sins…" The word "return" is right there in the verse.
Edom isn't named in this passage. The verse says, "They will return to Egypt." It follows God's words about remembering their iniquity and punishing their sins. Egypt is the answer.

A flood is a big, dramatic guess, but it isn't what the verse says. God says, "…I will send fire upon their cities, and it will consume their citadels." Fire is what He says He will send, not water. The citadels are what the fire consumes.

Locusts show up in other parts of the Bible, but not in this verse. God says, "…I will send fire upon their cities, and it will consume their citadels." Fire is the answer here. Right before that, the verse mentions Israel's palaces and Judah's fortified cities.
